title: Before the silver cord
hookLine: remember thy Creator in the days of thy youth, before the silver cord is loosed (Ecclesiastes 12:1–7)
tomorrow: so many texts on this shelf. what did each one ask of its readers?

cards: On moving day, a house goes quiet one room at a time. The rugs are up, voices echo, one last mug waits on the counter. The Preacher's last poem is about a house like that.
The keepers of the house tremble. The strong men bow. The grinders stop, because they are few.
Those who look out of the windows grow dark. The doors to the street are shut, the sound of the mill goes low, and the daughters of music are brought down.

teach.b: Whose house? Read slowly and you can hear it. The Talmud reads the poem as a body growing old: the grinders are teeth, the windows are eyes.

teach.h: THE SILVER CORD, THE GOLDEN BOWL.
teach.b: Then the end comes in pictures: "Or ever the silver cord be loosed, or the golden bowl be broken, or the pitcher be broken at the fountain." One picture: a lamp on its silver chain drops; a jar breaks at the well.

"Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it." A gentle word for parents listening with children: this is a poem about dying, told without fear.
And all of it hangs on its first line: "Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth." Here's the teaching. In Ecclesiastes, the honest look at aging isn't there to frighten.

teach.h: REMEMBER NOW, WHILE THE LAMP IS LIT.
teach.b: It's a call to turn toward God, and toward your life, now, while the lamp is still lit.
That's why the poem opens with remember. Worth repeating tonight: Ecclesiastes pictures growing old as a house going quiet, room by room, and the Preacher tells it so the day gets used.

how: Ecclesiastes 12 is read in Jewish and Christian tradition as a poem on aging and death; the Talmud reads its images as parts of the body, and its first line, 'remember now thy Creator', is read as a call to turn to God early in life.

games.q: what does “before the silver cord” mean?
o: remembering what matters while life is still here
a family heirloom handed down to the eldest
a rope that ties a boat safely to the shore

games.q: the quiet house: tap the pairs.

s: the poem in Ecclesiastes 12 opens with 'remember'
remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth.
Ecclesiastes 12 is written to frighten its readers
it looks at aging honestly so the days get used.
in 12:7 the spirit returns to God who gave it
the dust to the earth as it was, the spirit to God.

games.q: the Preacher is about to describe the quiet house and the broken bowl. what does he put first, before all of it?
o: remember thy Creator in the days of thy youth.
eat, drink and forget, for tomorrow we die.
count your years carefully, so nothing surprises you.
games.why: 12:1 opens the poem with remember: the honest picture of aging serves the call to turn toward God now.

practice: Choose one thing you've been putting off that matters more than it's urgent: a call to someone older, a question you've meant to ask, a place you've meant to see.
For these two minutes, picture doing it this week, while the lamp is lit. If you pray, you can hold the Preacher's words, remember now thy Creator; if not, simply hold the day you have.

wordCard.voice: Before the silver cord: the lamp on its silver chain, and the Preacher's call to remember while it still hangs.

orig.note: Hebrew: remember, the poem's first command in Ecclesiastes 12:1.

carryVoice: Keep this one: before the silver cord, so remember while the lamp is lit. See you tomorrow.
